(A self-limit: this is one scale among several, not the only gauge. A society also has readings for rule of law, technical capacity, institutional resilience — ethics is one ruler. This essay claims only that this ruler reads something true, not that it measures everything.)
3.2 First, Correct an Error That Invites a One-Line Rebuttal Now for a surgery. The original draft (or rather, a version many people love to tell) contained this claim: animals have no good and evil, no empathy, no responsibility; humans are the only beings that broke through instinct; ethics is the essential difference between humans and animals.
It sounds rousing. It doesn’t stand — and it’s the kind of not-standing that gets toppled by one line from anyone who knows the field.
Decades of observations by the primatologist Frans de Waal are on the table: capuchin monkeys faced with “same work, different pay” refuse their cucumber share; chimpanzees actively reconcile after violent conflict, grooming each other; elephants rescue distressed companions — in documented cases, some of the rescued were not kin. Empathy, reciprocity, a sense of fairness — the prototype of morality exists widely in the animal world. It is not humanity’s exclusive invention.
So “animals know no good and evil; only humans have ethics” cannot be printed as-is. Print it, and the first comment from a knowledgeable reader is “go read de Waal” — and that one line is enough to deflate the whole essay’s credibility.
3.3 So What Is Special About Humans: Not Doing Good — Quarreling Over Good But your intuition holds something true — on morality, humans and animals are indeed two kinds of beings. Only the dividing line sits somewhere else.
Animals have empathy, reciprocity, fairness-sense — but they do not quarrel over these things. A chimpanzee does not stop to ask: “Is this reconciliation actually fair? Should fairness follow effort or need?” The capuchin refuses the cucumber from an instinctive sense of unfairness, but it will not open a debate on “distributive justice,” let alone write the two camps’ positions into scriptures and transmit them for millennia.
Humans do. Humans are the only species that convenes a standing assembly on “should” and “ought” — and that assembly has been in session for thousands of years without adjourning:
“Sacrifice the few to save the many — right or wrong?” Some say yes; some say never. “Does the well-meant lie count as a lie?” Some say no; some say yes. “Does one keep faith with enemies too?” Some call it the bottom line; others call it cruelty to one’s own. No other animal splits into camps over “what does kindness mean” and quarrels for millennia, even goes to war over it. The prototype of morality, animals have. But the questioning, correcting, rebelling against, and remaking of morality itself — that is exclusively human. Other creatures live by instinctive reciprocity; humans refuse to stop at reciprocity — they must interrogate “what reciprocity is right,” then rewrite their own rules of behavior according to their answers, over and over.
So the meaning of “ethics defines the human” survives, with the blade re seated:
Humans are not the animals that do good. They are the animals that haggle with “good.” What defines the human is not ethics itself, but humanity’s never-ending interrogation of ethics.
This phrasing has an extra benefit — it no longer demeans animals, and it states ethics’ origin more precisely: precisely because the animal side already holds the raw material of empathy and reciprocity, ethics is not a set of commandments dropped from heaven. It is the animal’s existing reciprocal instinct, amplified, abstracted, and turned into principles that can be argued. An amplification, not an invention. So this essay dislikes the phrase “humans broke through instinct,” preferring: humanity took the small ember of reciprocity in instinct and fanned it into a fire large enough to illuminate and to conflagrate — it can light up civilization, and it can burn civilization down. Which is exactly the next section: when the fire grows, someone wants to own it.
IV. Ethics Has Factories, and Factories Have Owners 4.1 Ethics Is Not Only Ground Out — It Is Also Manufactured The foregoing — ethics is ground out — is correct but incomplete. Grinding is one source. There is another, and it has been gaining ground in the modern era: ethics is not only grown. It is also made, deliberately, by organization.
Think how you learned “what is right” — not entirely ground out in living; a large share was taught into you:
In primary school you recited “helping others is a virtue; lying is shameful”; At the company annual meeting, leadership taught you “wolf culture is drive; slacking is shameful”; On trending topics, cycle after cycle of “downfall — pile-on — social death” taught you “this is wrong, and doing it costs”; In prison, inmates are re-educated to “reform and start anew”; In advertising, brands repeat: “buying this is how you love your family.” These are not measures you ground out in dealing with people. They are designed and poured into you. The same behavior under a different value system gets a different label overnight: the same “don’t take losses” is taught as “shrewdness” in one place and “slyness” in another; the same “obedience” is “loyalty” in one organization and “servility” in another. The behavior is the behavior. The label is set by whoever pours.
So the essay’s second knife:
Ethics comes in two kinds: the ground-out kind and the manufactured kind. Any institution that can mass-shape a population’s sense of “what counts as right” — schools, companies, media, platforms, courts, prisons — is an ethics factory.
4.2 One Layer Deeper: Factories Have Owners This observation alone isn’t new — everyone knows schools teach conduct. The original draft stopped at the “positive energy” surface. This essay digs one layer deeper, because beneath this layer sits a question nobody is comfortable with, and nobody gets around:
If ethics is manufactured, there are factories; where there are factories, someone runs the factories — someone decides which “right” the assembly line produces.
Schools can teach self-sacrifice or teach obedience-supreme, depending on who writes the textbooks. Media can amplify one voice and mute another, depending on who holds the editor’s chair. Prisons can rehabilitate or destroy, depending on which theory of rehabilitation they execute. A platform’s trending list can crown one value system and, overnight, brand another “politically incorrect” — depending on whose hand stands behind the algorithm.
Whoever controls these factories is installing the factory defaults of good and evil into an entire generation — writing “what counts as right” into people’s base-layer settings before they can question anything. This is mightier than ordering people around: commands govern a moment; defaults govern a lifetime — and the poured-in mistake it for their own thinking.
Group-Side Observation asked, “Who supervises the rebuilder?” — that question aimed at power holders. This essay supplies the other half:
Who supervises the factory defaults of right and wrong? Power holders fight over power; ethics-factory owners fight over definition — and often, these are the same people doing both.
What a power holder wants most has never been the army. It is the definitional power that “my words are morality, and those who oppose me are degenerate.” With it, he need not persuade you one by one — he only needs society’s factories to manufacture “obedience to him” as “goodness.”
4.3 Nail the Boundaries Immediately, Before the Knife Cuts Its Own Having said “factories,” we must stop at once and nail the boundaries, or this essay slides into a conspiracy theory in which every school and institution deceives and all “manufactured ethics” is bad. Not so. Four points:
First: manufactured ethics is not automatically bad ethics. Public education teaching honesty, courts deterring breach, media promoting helping others — in many decent societies, the top-poured ethics points in the same direction as the folk-ground ethics. The school’s “don’t lie” and the street’s “don’t deceive” are the same thing. Here the factory is the pumping station’s amplifier, not its polluter.
Second: ground-out ethics is not automatically good either. The street-ground “don’t take advantage” is good. But some ground-out rules — “women shouldn’t be seen in public,” “outsiders are all thieves” — are bad rules, and precisely because they come “handed down from the ancestors,” they are extra-hard to change. Natively-ground ethics loses in being unwritten and brittle, and it loses in mistaking prejudice for tradition.
Third: the true watershed is not “ground” versus “made” — it is whether challenge is permitted. Ground-out ethics gets re-ground by new friction — this generation finds it wrong, the next grinds out a new one. Manufactured ethics, if it too can be discussed, overturned, remade, differs not at all in essence from the ground-out kind. What is truly dangerous is not “someone shaping ethics.” It is the shaper denying that he shapes — pouring, while proclaiming “this is heaven’s law, always has been, beyond question.” Whenever a set of ethics declares itself “beyond discussion, beyond change,” ask one more question: who taught you this sentence, and what are they after?
Fourth: nail the fourth point into a ruler — an ethics’ health is measured not by how correct it is, but by whether it leaves itself an opening for being overturned. Ethics that permits challenge can be corrected when wrong. Ethics that forbids challenge rots even when right — because it stays forever in the era that invented it, unable to follow new human circumstances.
Finally, one rule carried over from the origin essay, so no reader uses this essay for point-scoring: it names no specific factory, institution, or era — it describes mechanisms, not labels. Whoever puts the “factory owner” hat onto a specific real-world unit misuses this essay. This is an observation lens, not a verdict.
4.4 Back to the Water: What Ethics Fears Is Not Supply Cuts — It Is a Single Source Assemble the four sections and return to the main line: ethics supplies trust’s water.
Ground-out ethics is countless small neighborhood water plants supplying: each house has its own measures; if one household’s rules grow badly, the neighbor still has other water. This “distributed supply” looks messy, but it survives cuts — one pipe cracks, the others still flow.
Manufactured ethics is the metropolitan water plant: efficient, wide coverage, capable of switching an entire nation onto one “right and wrong” overnight. But this centralized supply has one fatal weakness — once the plant’s owner takes the source, or the plant produces a defective batch, everyone drinks the contamination, and with only one producer, even the option of “switching suppliers” doesn’t exist.
So this essay’s attitude toward “ethics factories” is not anti-factory. It is anti-monopoly:
What ethics’ supply fears most is not factories everywhere. It is this-and-only-this. The ground, the taught, the argued-and-corrected — many channels supply; one channel breaks, the others hold. A single-source right-and-wrong, once wrong, is a whole society drinking dirty water with nowhere to switch.
This is also why “quarreling over good” is so precious — the quarreling is those small folk water plants continuously producing new sources. A society that lets ethics be publicly argued keeps all its small plants open. A society that strangles argument and permits one voice welds every pipe into one. The former is messy, but it survives. The latter is tidy — and when the one pipe breaks, everything breaks.
Epilogue: Turning the Lamp on Myself Written this far, by the old custom, the final step is turning the lamp on myself.
This essay claimed ethics is trust’s water line, that boundaries are ground out, that ethics has factories, that owners fight over definition. So — who is saying these words?
Someone living through a water outage.
My generation happens to live in an era of “predictability supply cuts” — today a guru collapses, tomorrow a conscientious company blows up, the day after a single post leaves someone with no way to defend themselves. Precisely because I stand at the scene of the outage, I turned to look at how the pipes were laid. In an era with ample security, ethics would be like air — no one would write a treatise “On Air,” because it is too natural, natural to the point of needing no explanation. So this essay is not transcendent truth. It is a maintenance report written from inside a water outage. It is useful because it stands at the same outage as its readers. The day the water comes back, it will probably look superfluous — which would be a good thing.
And a falsification opening must be left, so this essay does not become the “beyond-discussion ethics” it criticizes.
The essay’s entire claim compresses to one sentence: ethics is society’s trunk production line supplying “behavioral predictability”; it is ground out of group friction and also manufactured in batches by factories; its mark of health is permitting many supply channels — and permitting itself to be overturned.
This sentence holds under conditions. If a society could be found — ethics widely dissolved, everyone harboring schemes — where predictability nonetheless stayed abundant for the long term, with all mutual trust carried by pure law, pure institutions, pure technology, then this essay’s framework fails; the water line is not a necessity. The shape I keep seeing so far: not found. Wherever ethics suffers mass supply cuts, law and institutions overload at the same time.
Someone will surely raise ratings, contracts, blockchain — technology can already replace ethics. This essay’s reply: the water technology supplies governs narrow-domain transactions — payments, fulfillment, ordering, inspection; bounded exchanges that contracts and ratings genuinely handle. But the bulk of human trust was never in the narrow domain: marriage and funerals, raising children, entrusting a life-threatening illness, handing your house keys to a stranger at midnight — these general domains have no black on white and no rating dimensions; smart contracts cannot encode them. Technology reaches the counter. Ethics’ cheap water supplies the vast ground technology cannot reach.
But I do not treat “not found yet” as “nonexistent.” If you find such a society — you are welcome to overturn me.
Finally, nailing down the relationships among the essays, closing the circuit of the series:
The origin essay asked: what does the individual trust machine live on? Answer: predictability. This essay asked: who produces predictability? Answer: ethics, the water line. Precondition Theory and Group-Side Observation asked: when the water is cut, how does the individual walk, and where does the era go?
Four essays, one thread — supply, demand, individual, group. Strung on one thread they form a complete map; pulled apart, each is only a corner of it.
This essay ends here. The rest is left to the people living through the outage to verify: of the “keeping one’s word” around you, how much rides on ground-out tacit understanding, and how much on poured-in rules? And that sentence you believe most firmly — “this is right” — who put it into your head, and when?
After the Lamp Turns: The System’s Final Chapter The main text closes on “turning the lamp on myself”: go verify the tacit understandings and rules around you. But what exactly does the lamp reveal once it turns? Why is ethics forever late to new situations? Why do humans quarrel fiercely over “good”? And how should ordinary people inside the vacuum period act? 👉 Read the system’s final chapter: On Ethics · Addendum — Ethics Is Always Late, and Society Keeps Rebuilding It →
Further Reading The system’s final chapter (after the lamp turns): On Ethics · Addendum — Ethics Is Always Late, and Society Keeps Rebuilding It — from profitable to ought, why humans quarrel over good, the contest for the norm vacuum, and ordinary people keeping the water flowing Next, the demand side: The Origin of Trust — what the trust machine lives on: predictability. The water line in this essay feeds that machine The individual mirror: Trust Crisis · Precondition Theory — how to walk through the vacuum period: six pits, five currents; weighing, avoiding, riding The group mirror: Trust Crisis · Group-Side Observation — where the era goes in the recasting period: seven symptoms, one sociological index This essay also has an audiobook version (6 episodes, 32 minutes), playing continuously with seven other books on the audiobook page.
Completed September 2026. This essay is a model, not moral preaching — every mechanism in it is a tool for understanding, not a law of history; of the same origin and scale as The Origin of Trust: every claim carries its preconditions first. It describes mechanisms and names no specific factory, institution, or era — this is an observation lens, not a verdict.

content:
Trust series · Origin (the foundational outline). The individual side covers “how you should walk”; the group side covers “where the era is heading.” Neither answers the more fundamental question: What is trust? Why must people trust? When trust collapses, why does it push people to two extremes? And why can this crack never be sewn shut in a lifetime? This piece supplies that foundation. Positioning: this is not a supplement to the other two essays — it is their common ground. Once it is in place, the “vacuum period” and the “recasting period” stop being asserted facts and become derivable conclusions. Reading order: not mandatory. To build the coordinate system first, start here. To see conclusions first, read the individual and group essays and come back — this piece nails their assertions into conclusions. The three interlock. Four writing rules: ① this is a model, not a law of history — a tool for understanding, not an object of faith; ② every universal claim carries its own limits — “I have repeatedly seen this shape” replaces “it has always been so”; ③ this essay takes no side — quite the opposite: what it shows is that the two torn ends share the same lesion; ④ it uses no private engineering cases, only everyday experience common to all humanity as anchor points.
0. Opening: Catch an Unthinking Gesture First In an elevator, a stranger finishes tapping his badge and hands you what he’s holding, asking you to hold it for a second. You take it.
You’re standing in a queue with a complete stranger behind you. You are not guarding against him at all times — you default to the assumption that he’s just standing in line, that he won’t suddenly do anything. You wait, at ease.
These are two things you do every day without ever asking why. They share one feature: no deliberation. You never ran an analysis of “is this person trustworthy” — your hand was already out.
But the same action, in a different setting, flips your reflex instantly. Late at night at an intersection, a stranger walks toward you; on the phone, a stranger asks you to read out your verification code. Now your body alerts before your brain does — muscles tighten, hair stands up, and the machine called “trust” delivers a verdict in a fraction of a second: unpredictable, withdraw.
Notice the detail: receiving the object and guarding against the stranger happen in the same person. It’s not that this person trusts some people and guards against others — it is one machine, switching outputs rapidly depending on context. That machine is the protagonist of this essay. What this essay takes apart is the machine itself: where it comes from, what it runs on, and what happens when it breaks.
Phenomena first, naming second. Now we begin naming.
I. Reasoning from Instinct: Trust Is a Survival Apparatus, Not a Moral Virtue 1.1 The Species’ Factory Settings Start with a fact that isn’t romantic: the human species is not born capable of living as an individual unit.
No fangs or claws, slower than most prey, an appallingly long childhood — an isolated human can neither gather enough food, nor protect children, nor survive several winters. Humans survived not because individuals are strong, but because humans invented a way of survival called “the group”: division of labor, cooperation, mutual lifting. One person hunts; a group drives the hunt. One person keeps watch; a group sleeps.
So note the order here: it is not “the individual surrenders to the group.” It is: the individual’s route to survival must itself pass through the group. Gregariousness is not a preference; it is this species’ way of surviving, period. We usually treat “social animal” as a biology label, but its meaning is concrete: part of your food, your safety, and your offspring is never held in your hands. It is held in other people’s hands.
1.2 The Hidden Cost of Living in Groups This is the cost of gregarious life, and the most easily missed: once you live at the scale of the group, you are, at every moment, handing part of your life to others.
After handing it over — on what basis do you stay alive?
There is only one answer: you must be able to judge “how will others treat me.”
Others’ behavior predictable → you can plan → you dare cooperate → you live; Others’ behavior unpredictable → you cannot plan → every act of giving might be fed to the dogs → you dare not cooperate → you cannot survive. So here is the nail this essay drives in:
Trust is a gregarious species’ dependence on the predictability of others’ behavior. It is not a moral virtue. It is a survival apparatus.
More trust or less trust is, at bottom, higher or lower predictability. A “trust-abundant” society is not one with better people; it is one whose behavioral system is more predictable — what you hand out will most likely be caught; what you sign will most likely be honored. A “trust-thin” society is not one with worse people; its behavioral system has become unpredictable — the same action, and the outcome is a lottery.
1.3 Then What About Morality, Integrity, Goodwill? They are parts on this apparatus, not the apparatus itself.
People prize honesty, promise-keeping, and kindness not because they are sublime beyond utility, but because they have an extremely practical effect: they make others’ behavior computable. A person who keeps promises is predictable to you; a person of goodwill requires no guard in advance. Morality’s real social function is to supply predictability.
Mistaking the part for the whole is the first misunderstanding this essay dismantles. We are used to saying “this person has no morals,” as if the root of the trust problem were moral decline. But morality is the lubricant that maintains predictability, not the chassis itself. The chassis is another layer. That layer is what the next section takes apart.
1.4 Clearing the Ground of a Misreading Luhmann, Zheng Yefu, and Fukuyama have thoroughly argued trust’s function for society. This essay will not repeat the consensus that “trust is a useful social mechanism” — it is already public property. What this essay wants to cut open are two under-explored things: what happens after this survival apparatus breaks down; and why, once a security model is written in, it is extraordinarily hard to rewrite. The public bones belong to the public; these two cuts are what this series aims to add.
II. Collapse: Predictability Snaps, and People Panic First 2.1 What a Trust Crisis Actually Is We can now define “trust crisis” without vagueness:
A trust crisis is not that human hearts turned bad. It is that the supply of predictability got cut off.
The old sources of predictability — acquaintances’ guarantees, reputation, personas, verbal promises, authoritative endorsements — fail en masse; the new sources — contracts, evidence, process, third-party verification — have not yet grown up to catch people. The interval in which you can rely on neither is what the other two essays call the vacuum period (individual side) and the recasting period (group side): the two sides of the same window.
By this point it has finally stopped being an asserted fact and become a derived conclusion: predictability supply cut → no one can plan → no one dares cooperate → defense, guard, and suspicion become the default. The age of peak suspicion is not the age of the worst hearts; it is the age when the survival chain is most thoroughly severed.
2.2 Suspicion Is Expensive, Low-Grade Fuel Here is a mechanism worth pausing on: when the supply of predictability is cut, a person does not cancel the need “I need predictability.” The need remains. It is still hungry. It merely switches to a low-grade fuel.
That low-grade fuel is called suspicion. Its logic: if I default to “no one can be trusted,” then at least “he is probably untrustworthy” is a stable expectation — I can at least plan on that basis (full defense). So suspicion is not the absence of defense; quite the opposite, it is an extremely expensive predictability purchased with defense: every act of guarding is wear, every confirmation of “untrustworthy, as expected” is self-verification. When trust goes hungry, what people stuff into the machine is precisely this fuel that makes it hungrier the more you feed it.
This explains something you have long observed: why the defensive attrition and emotional overdraft of a crisis era cannot be stopped. Because it is not a bad habit — it is a starving machine eating low-grade fuel. You cannot fill a starving machine by “telling people to be optimistic.” You have to first let the machine believe the grain is coming.
A boundary, so suspicion isn’t painted as pure error: in environments where predictability is genuinely low, moderate suspicion is a necessary survival strategy, not a defect. Its only problem is one thing — being adopted as the permanent default. “Guard first” as an occasional response is useful; “no one can be trusted” as a factory setting, and the attrition never stops. Whether suspicion helps depends on preconditions — that sentence itself is condition theory.
2.3 Why Reasoning With People Fails at This Moment Here is this section’s most uncomfortable inference: when a person’s survival chassis is shaking, telling them “you should believe in good things” is like telling a drowning person “relax first.”
It is not that they refuse to trust. It is that they dare not. In an environment where predictability has been cut off, trust is not a choice for them; it is a survival risk. We often misread this “daring not to trust” as coldness, cynicism, moral decline — and then blame each other’s hearts. But in this essay’s framework, that is a survival system protecting itself: it would rather starve than stake its last chips on an unpredictable world.
Seeing this clearly is the ground for everything that follows: a trust crisis is, first, a survival event; only second, a moral event. Get the order backwards and every prescription will be wrong.
III. Divergence: When the Chassis Shakes, People Run to the Two Ends 3.1 The Question Everyone Must Answer When the chassis shakes, everyone is forced to answer the same question: which side do I stake my chips on?
Note: this is not a moral exam. It is a survival exam. And most people don’t answer it by thinking — the answer snaps out of them, the way receiving the parcel or guarding against the stranger does. No deliberation.
Let us fix the limits first, so this isn’t misread as “the world has only two kinds of people”: the people who actually reach the two extreme endpoints are a minority. The overwhelming majority stand in the middle — rule-abiding in some situations, tempted across the line by some temptations; craving order, yet afraid of extreme measures. These two “camps” are not two portraits of people; they are two forces. Their real use is to illuminate the two pulling forces inside everyone in the middle. See the two endpoints clearly, and how the middle gets pulled is all clear.
3.2 One End: The Profit-Through-Decay Camp The first force points this way: since no one keeps the rules anymore, I will be the one who doesn’t.
This is the most easily misunderstood camp — we usually just call them “bad.” But in this essay’s framework they are not merely a moral option; they are a survival mode. The ingenuity and the viciousness of this mode live in the same place: what he earns is, in fact, the money of “other people still keeping the rules.”
In a vacuum of order, the rule-abiding become predictable, and the predictable become harvestable. What the line-breaker harvests is precisely the rule-keeper’s predictability: others keep promises, so he can defraud; others queue, so he can cut in; others are honest, so he can squeeze. He turns other people’s rule-keeping into his own revenue source.
And this mode has a deeper property: it feeds itself by lowering everyone else’s survival chassis. Predatory survival is not satisfied with a one-time kill; it wants a sustained harvesting source — and for the source to persist, the harvested must be kept in a “harvestable” state. So in environments where it holds the advantage, the common shape is: people become poorer, more dependent, less able to leave. This is not to say every predator deliberately manufactures poverty (that would be motive-guessing); it is to say the structure of harvesting naturally trends toward this outcome. The more miserable the harvested, the stabler the harvester. So this camp is not merely “going bad.” It is remodeling the environment into a shape that is easier to harvest.
(A limit: this describes no particular country or era. It describes a mechanism. Anywhere in a vacuum of order, any gain obtained by “turning others into harvestable objects” is this mechanism running. The small things around you and the large things in history are the same engine.)
3.3 The Other End: The Obsessive-Order Camp The second force points exactly the opposite way: I cannot endure the chaos for one more day. Order must be taken back by the most thorough means.
This camp is also commonly misread — we say they are “too extreme,” “black-and-white thinkers.” But in this essay’s framework, his craving for order is not fastidiousness. It is fear: in an unpredictable world, he cannot survive. Gray is not, for him, “tolerable ambiguity.” It is “the abyss of the unpredictable.” So he demands an absolute, black-and-white order that purges every shade of gray — because gray equals unpredictable, and unpredictable equals death.
He is willing to use the most extreme means for this, including war. Not because he thirsts for blood, but because on the scale in his chest, order outranks everything — including people. In his eyes, to end the unpredictable, any cost is acceptable. He is not committing evil for its own sake; he is saving himself by means of evil, and he sincerely believes it is salvation.
Here a bridge must be built first, so we don’t jump straight from “one person’s fear” to “collective war”: the one willing to take up arms is never an isolated obsessive. The model is not a private possession — the same era pours the same unease into an entire generation’s bodies (next section). Only when a crowd carrying the same model presses the switch together does fear acquire the scale of war.
One clarification, to avoid misfiring: pursuing order, hoping to rebuild predictability — nothing wrong with that in itself. The core lesion of the obsessive-order camp is not “wanting order.” It is believing one path: that risk can be eliminated once and for all by thoroughly purging every gray zone, every uncertain individual. Ordinary people expecting rules, contracts, justice — that is a healthy demand, a different thing from the lesion. Only when a person concludes “to eliminate uncertainty, I must eliminate the people who carry uncertainty” does he fall into this model.
Within this camp, one more split: those who genuinely want to rebuild order, and those who use order as a pretext to seize power. The former are fear-driven; the latter power-driven. The terrifying part is that both end in the same motion — because once a genuine rebuilder takes over “the rebuilding,” his own model pushes him forward (the mechanism, next section). So the question in the group-side essay — “who supervises the rebuilder?” — is not a reminder. It is a necessary question the model’s mechanism forces into existence.
3.4 The Central Cut: Two Extremes, One Lesion Now comes this essay’s most important cut:
The profit-through-decay camp and the obsessive-order camp are not the opposition of good and evil. They are the two extremes flung out when the same survival chassis shattered.
The two camps share one lesion — insecurity. Both believe they are saving themselves; in fact both chase the same thing by opposite means: safety. The decay camp seeks safety by “freeing myself from all rules”; the order camp seeks safety by “subjecting everything to absolute rules.” One wants to demolish rules, one wants to weld rules shut — but what they fear is the same thing: rules failing, the world turning unpredictable.
The meaning of this cut: in a torn era, you stop joining any team. When you watch the two sides curse each other, what you see is not “who is more right.” You see two wounded people in the same hospital room, fighting over the same bottle of medicine by hurting each other.
A deeper observation: the two poles feed each other. The chaos the decay camp manufactures feeds the order camp’s fear; the order camp’s purges manufacture new victims and new chaos, handing knives to the decay camp. The split itself is how the two forces maintain each other. So once the split begins, it cannot be stopped by persuasion — its fuel is the shared fear of both crowds.
You don’t need to wait for a war to see this loop. Take a homeowners’ group in one residential compound where property management has changed hands several times: each change brings a round of settling accounts with the old firm, a round of watchfulness toward the new one; eventually, whenever anyone proposes anything, the first comment is “what’s his angle.” No war, no purges — the same mutually-feeding loop, turning as smoothly at the scale of a few hundred households as it ever did in history.
IV. Fixation: Why This Crack Never Closes in a Lifetime 4.1 The Security Model: Written Once At this point one deeper question remains unanswered: why are these two extremes so stubborn? Why does history replay the same script while every generation jumps into the same pit?
The answer is one word: model.
Every era pours a “security model” into its people. This model specifies the most basic default settings: what kind of world counts as safe, who is trustworthy, who should be guarded against, whom to suspect first when things go wrong, whether people are by default benign or by default dangerous.
These defaults are not thought out. They are written directly into the body, during a person’s formative years, by the real conditions of the environment. Those whose youth was stable carry models reading “the world is safe by default; people are benign by default.” Those whose youth was turbulent carry models reading “people cannot be trusted; survival first.” One great upheaval brands the same groove into an entire generation’s bodies.
This language of “model / pour-in / repaint” belongs to the same family as the “instinct-hijack / checkpoints / ruler” set in The Inner Side of Happiness (《幸福的内在》): there, the program is what the species pours into every person; here, it is what the era pours into every generation. Two pours, one mechanism. The difference is scale: instinct took hundreds of millions of years to write; the security model takes only decades — but it, too, walks with you to the end of life.
4.2 Left Hand, Right Hand: Irreversible for Life And once this model is written in, it is irreversible for life. This is the essay’s central mirror — your dominant hand:
Just as you can never switch from your right hand once you’ve habituated it. You can train your left hand to assist, train it to be quite dexterous — but in the instant of writing, eating, or grabbing for your life, what shoots out is the right hand. The security model works the same way: later refinement, reading, awakening — all of it is repainting. It does not touch the foundation. Repainting is not useless — it makes behavior decent, lets a person observe themselves — but it cannot change the foundation’s shape.
What you expose in your most panicked instant is forever the base color your era poured. A person who grew up in turmoil, who then spent a lifetime reading and cultivating until his speech and bearing were transformed — in the instant he hears a strange noise at night, he is still the person who “reaches for the knife first.” Not because he is a hypocrite, but because that is how his foundation was poured.
“Irreversible for life” is meant functionally, not as a neuroscience claim: you cannot return to the “never-poured” state — your immediate reactions will keep defaulting to the old track. But the brain can learn new things; you can absolutely learn to pause one more second after the reaction, to ask one more question. What is irreversible is the primer, not the cloth itself.
This explains something: why two people can read the same new event in nearly opposite ways and neither can persuade the other. It is not right versus wrong; it is two models outputting. The one raised in turmoil reads “it’s starting again — hide.” The one raised in safety reads “let’s look first — probably nothing.” Both believe they are awake. Both are being translated by their own models.
4.3 Outside First, Then Inside: Why Purges Cannot Stop With this model, look again at that recurring shape in history so often attributed to “power struggle” or “unknowable hearts,” and it becomes much clearer.
I have repeatedly seen the same shape: a rebuilder of order comes to power and first purges the visible dissenters — the obviously different, the disobedient, those who threaten order. Once the surface is uniform and everyone is “one of us,” the purge does not stop. It turns inward, hunting among his own for “those who might think differently.”
Why can’t it stop?
Because this purge machine’s engine is not external. It sits inside him, in the location of his own insecurity. What he wants is “everything under my control, no source of uncertainty anywhere.” But the real source of uncertainty is not outside. It is that spot in his own chest that forever feels some fish slipped the net. So the process is necessarily: purge the outside, the targets run out, the unease remains; he then manufactures a new target inside and keeps purging. Outside first, then inside; inside has no bottom.
Here we can connect to Girard’s scapegoat mechanism — humans need an identifiable “source of calamity” to carry anxiety that has nowhere else to go. What this essay wants to point at is the engine behind the scapegoat: the self-maintenance of the insecurity model. For the model to live, it must keep finding evidence that “a threat remains”; if it cannot find one, it manufactures one. This is not the evil of some individual. It is an automated process of a wounded model.
4.4 The Boundaries That Must Be Nailed Down Having come this far, we must stop and nail the boundaries down, or this essay will slide somewhere it should not go.
First: this is a recurring shape, not an iron law. Human history also has eras with relatively healthy models that did not maintain themselves through purges. Whether a model is healthy depends on whether an era held up its people’s supply of security — where supply was ample, the model did not need to manufacture enemies; where supply was cut, the model found an enemy for everyone. Do not read it as “every dynasty did this.” Read it as: whenever security supply is cut, this shape raises its head.
Second: this essay evaluates no specific regime or figure. It describes a mechanism; it attaches no label. Any reading that tries to fit this framework onto a specific contemporary target misuses it — this is an observation lens, not a verdict. This rule is the same one written in the group-side essay.
Third: the value of seeing the mechanism clearly is precisely its use. Because if the security model maintains itself by “manufacturing enemies,” then any narrative proclaiming “there is one common enemy; purge it and we are safe” deserves one extra question: is it solving insecurity, or feeding its own model? That question extends the fifth question of your precondition theory — whose hands does it put the microphone into?
Fourth: this is a model, not the whole explanation of history. Real historical events are always the layered product of power contests, conflicts of interest, external wars, institutional inertia — never driven by one psychological model alone. This essay extracts one driving force — usually the one hiding behind every banner — but it never pretends to be the whole. Reducing everything to “the security model” is the same over-simplification, and this essay will not carry that bag.
Finally: leave the model an opening for being overturned. Its validity has conditions: if a large number of cases of order-rebuilding under security famine that did not slide into purges can be found, this shape fails. A model that writes out its own falsification conditions qualifies as a tool — is that not exactly what your precondition theory teaches?
V. Turning the Lamp on Myself: The “I” Writing This Also Carries a Model At the close, one thing must be done: turn the lamp on myself.
In section one I said “trust is a survival apparatus.” In section three, “two extremes, one lesion.” In section four, “the model is written once and is irreversible.” So — who is speaking these words?
A model poured out by some era is speaking.
That I can see the “survival / predictability” layer at all is very likely because my own generation lives at the scene of predictability’s fracture. The scene let me see the chassis. In an era with ample security, perhaps no one would ever feel that “trust” needed to be specifically taken apart — it would be too natural, natural to the point of needing no explanation. So this essay is not transcendent truth. It is a model carrying its era’s body heat. It is useful because it stands on the same scene as its readers. It will not be useful forever.
But knowing the model exists is the model’s only escape hatch.
I cannot change my foundation — the dominant hand cannot change. But I know which foundation I stand on. So after “the most panicked instant” has passed, I can say one sentence to that instant’s reaction: that was my era speaking, not me. That sentence buys a little room to maneuver: I cannot block my first reaction, but I need not mistake my first reaction for the whole of “me.” Repainting does not move the foundation — but the person repainting at least knows what ground lies under their feet.
This “model” has an even deeper home: it is your precondition theory, in its version inside the human heart. Precondition theory says the era sets preconditions for thought — conditions must match for it to hold. This essay says the era also sets preconditions for every person — not at the level of thought, but at the level of security. Behind a person’s judgments, positions, and alignments there stand not only social conditions but the security conditions written in early. Two sets of conditions speak at once; count only the former and you will miss a person’s deepest reason for taking a side.
This is also why the trust block has three essays. Seeing the origin clearly (this essay), the individual side knows where to stand (how to change currency, how to avoid pits and ride momentum), and the group side becomes legible (how to read where the era goes). The origin essay is not a “first layer of truth” pressing down from above. It is the ground that keeps the other two from hanging in the air.
Epilogue: A Question Left for the Reader This essay described a machine: it runs on predictability; when supply is cut it starves; starving, it runs to the two ends; and the shape of its running gets welded in by the model.
Finally, by the custom of this site, the other half is left to the people living inside it:
What is your “that instant”? — At what moment did you first feel “this world is no longer the one I grew up young in”? That was the first time your model got nudged by the era.
We provide no standard answer. Because the answer is not in the essay; it is in tens of thousands of real lives. Once you see your own model clearly, it stops being “fate” and becomes a “known condition” — conditions cannot be changed, but knowing where the conditions are, a person can decide where to put their foot down.
Further Reading For the sentence left unfinished here: Trust · On Ethics (upstream · the supply side) — section 1.3 said “morality is a part, not the chassis; that layer is dismantled in the next section.” That dismantling lives there. Read it first, then return for the foundation: Trust Crisis · Precondition Theory (individual side) — how to walk through the vacuum period: six pits, five currents; weighing, avoiding, riding. Then the group half: Trust Crisis · Group-Side Observation (group side) — where the era goes in the recasting period: seven symptoms, one sociological index. Dig deeper downward: The Ladder of Civilization — feeding and cooperation: why trust is the foundation of this civilized ground. This essay also has an audiobook version (7 episodes, 26 minutes), playing continuously with seven other books on the audiobook page.
Completed September 2026. This essay is a model, not a law of history — every mechanism in it is a tool for understanding; of the same origin and scale as Trust Crisis · Precondition Theory and Trust Crisis · Group-Side Observation: every claim carries its preconditions first.
summary: Trust series · Origin (the foundational outline). The individual side covers “how you should walk”; the group side covers “where the era is heading.” Neither answers the more fundamental question: What is trust? Why must people trust? When trust collapses, why does it push people to two extremes? And why can this crack never be sewn shut in a lifetime? This piece supplies that foundation. Positioning: this is not a supplement to the other two essays — it is their common ground. Once it is in place, the “vacuum period” and the “recasting period” stop being asserted facts and become derivable conclusions. Reading order: not mandatory. To build the coordinate system first, start here. To see conclusions first, read the individual and group essays and come back — this piece nails their assertions into conclusions. The three interlock. Four writing rules: ① this is a model, not a law of history — a tool for understanding, not an object of faith; ② every universal claim carries its own limits — “I have repeatedly seen this shape” replaces “it has always been so”; ③ this essay takes no side — quite the opposite: what it shows is that the two torn ends share the same lesion; ④ it uses no private engineering cases, only everyday experience common to all humanity as anchor points.
title: Trust Is Not Morality; It Is the Chassis of Survival: The Origin of Trust

content:
Era Observation · opening essay. The column’s charter: no chasing hot-topic emotions; only analytical frameworks are given, and the framework will keep being applied to collective trust events (update rhythm at the end). This essay is the group mirror of Trust Crisis · Precondition Theory (the individual side): the individual side covered “how you walk within the era”; this one covers “where the era itself is heading.” No predictions, no verdicts — only an observation framework. Best read after the individual side (pit-avoidance + riding momentum); new readers are advised to read that first and return here. Method: signal → index → calibration → boundaries — section 2 captures signals, section 3 matches indexes, section 4 calibrates and sets boundaries, section 5 returns to the individual. The framework unfolds in self-contained fashion; no outside material needed.
0. The 30-Second Version The situation: the old trust system is failing as a whole; society has entered the credit-recasting period (the individual side calls it the “vacuum period” — the two sides of the same window). The tool: a “signal → index → boundary” analytical framework. No predictions, no verdicts. The stance: an individual doing verifiable things and occupying the “verifier” position is supplying raw material for the recasting. ⚠️ The one-sentence standing prohibition: do not read this as a doomsday prophecy — the recasting period is labor pain, not the end. Things are breaking, and things are growing.
I. The Individual Side Covered “How You Walk.” One Question Remains Unanswered Trust Crisis · Precondition Theory fully covered the individual half. Six gun muzzles, five appreciating assets, three rulers, plus one landing point: measure the world with Sartre’s ruler outward; guard yourself with Levinas’s line inward. It answered “how does a person walk in this era.”
But when readers close the book, another question most likely surfaces: changing currency is easy for me alone — but what about society? What state is the whole era actually in? Those collapses, blowups, plot reversals, self-proofs — taken together, are they a pile of coincidences, or a structure?
This essay answers that question. It is the mirror of the individual side: the individual side covered “where a person stands”; this covers “where the era is going.”
Rules first, so it isn’t misread. It is not current-affairs commentary — it takes no side and condemns no one. It is not a forecast — it cannot say whether tomorrow is better or worse. It is an observation framework: put the collective phenomena you see into it, and you know what they are, where they came from, where they tend, and what you can do. The framework is a tool, not a conclusion.
One term-alignment to pin down first: the individual side says “vacuum period”; the group side says “recasting period” — the two sides of the same window, not two events. Hold onto that window; the seven phenomena below are all the weather outside it.
II. The Phenomena First: What the Group Is Going Through Watch a month of trending topics on your phone and seven recurring shapes assemble themselves. They are not isolated news items; they are the seven symptoms of one illness.
1. Institutional credit went bankrupt first When an institution speaks, our first reaction is no longer “check whether it’s true” but “don’t swallow it whole.” The Evergrande real-estate collapse (2021 debt blowup) — the promises, contracts, and credit of a trillion-yuan enterprise went to zero overnight, and ordinary people’s life savings were zeroed out with them. Since then, the phrase “in black and white” carries less weight. This is the Tacitus Trap: once public credit is overdrawn far enough, nothing an institution says is believed. The organizational layer and the narrative layer are hemorrhaging as a whole.
2. Public opinion started flipping three times a day One event: one version in the morning, a reversal in the afternoon, another by night. The Yan Dongping case (a late-2024 Beijing divorce trial) — a one-sided narrative of “ten years of feeling” could turn ten years of sacrifice overnight into “a calculated scheme.” Truth is no longer discovered; it is “produced.” The group is pushed along by emotion; truth is diluted into “versions.” You cannot be sure which version is true — only that the next reversal is on its way.
3. The moral high ground collapsed systematically Even “doing good” is no longer credible by default. Han Hong’s charity has faced sustained questioning (since 2020 pandemic donations) — from where the money went to her motives, everything demands self-proof. Charities must prove innocence first; the cost of goodwill has been bid up to a historic high. Public welfare and charity, once emotional trusts, are now all on the “suspect first, verify later” list. When the moral high ground collapses, the people standing on it fall loudest.
4. People retreated into small screens Work units, neighborhoods, acquaintances — the old communities were our grandparents’ “trust containers”: your reputation and your credit had witnesses. Now these containers are dissolving; people have retreated into their separate little screens, and the entity they talk to most each day is the phone. Fewer people around who can vouch for you; more algorithm-fed echo chambers. Humans are physically closer and trust- lonelier.
5. Not hunger — “why should I” This generation’s material conditions are nowhere near the hunger of the previous one. Yet “lying flat” and “going-crazy literature” became a generation’s emotional outlets — not hunger, but suffocation. The gap between expectation and reality keeps widening: the rules say “everyone has a chance”; reality says “chance has a threshold.” Tocqueville pointed at this mechanism more than a century and a half ago: upheaval tends not to come at the poorest moment, but when life has just begun improving and expectations have just been raised — he was observing France at the end of the 18th century (the famous claim in The Old Regime and the Revolution), but the mechanism of “expectations lifted, reality lagging, tempers flaring” is recurring weather in this window. Expectations go up, reality can’t keep up, and the mood turns febrile.
6. No one dares move first Public affairs keep getting colder. Fundraisers must prove themselves repeatedly before anyone donates; no one takes the lead in community matters; everyone waits for someone else to move. This is not all apathy — in a trust-crisis era, the first mover bears all the risk while the benefits may be shared by all. So everyone tacitly chooses: wait. Collective action is paralyzed; free-riding becomes the default rationality. Olson called it “the collective action problem”: it is not that no one suffers — it is that no one has the incentive to pay the cost first.
7. Trust migrated from “institutions” to “persons” Trust in institutions collapsed, but trust must live somewhere. So it migrated onto “persons”: Luo Yonghao (founder of Smartisan, six hundred million in debt, repaid it live-stream by live-stream, the whole “true repayment” chronicle public) — paying your debts became this era’s scarcest credit asset. Various “conscientious entrepreneurs” and “grassroots idols” are celebrated not because their institutions are reliable but because they “seem like a person.” Meanwhile people split into camps by identity: fandoms, regions, professions, consumption patterns — when the whole society can’t be trusted, hug your own crowd first. Identity clustering is the psychological compensation of a trust crisis.
Seven symptoms, one mnemonic: institutions fall, opinion flips, morals crash, atoms scatter, the gap widens, no one moves, trust moves to persons. They are not seven accidental misfortunes — lay the structure out and you’ll find they point at one thing.
III. Not Chaos — the Old Trust System Is Failing Put the seven symptoms into a sociological index and their identities become clear:
Symptom Corresponding theory Role it plays Institutional credit bankruptcy / moral high-ground collapse Durkheim · anomie Old norms (integrity/goodwill/authority) collapsed, new ones not yet formed — structural necrosis of the trust infrastructure Triple daily reversals / emotional contagion Tarde · laws of imitation (+ Le Bon, with care) How ideas and emotions spread through crowds — transmission itself became the dominant force Not hunger — “why should I” Tocqueville · expectation gap The igniter — fairness breached, tempers febrile No one dares move first Olson · collective action The consequence — missing trust makes repair extremely hard Trust migrating to “persons” / identity clustering Weber · charisma / status groups The compensation — institutions failing, people retreat to persons and identity (Background) rich-poor, class, distribution Marx · material institutions The base — always present, but rarely the direct detonator (The plea) rebuild order, question legitimacy Rousseau · social contract The wish hanging overhead — and the easiest for power to exploit The seven symptoms are not seven diseases; they are different faces of one lesion. Together, one sentence:
A trust crisis at the group level = anomie (Durkheim) × opinion contagion (Tarde) × expectation gap (Tocqueville), triple-stacked. The base is material institutions; the surface forms are paralyzed collective action and identity clustering; hanging overhead is the plea to “rebuild the contract.”
But note: this is a first-pass triage, not a diagnosis. One symptom can map to several indexes; one index can explain several symptoms; reality is a web — this one-to-one table is the reader’s starter version, not an exhaustive truth. For the general reader it also translates to one sentence:
Old norms rotted × rumors travel fast × everyone’s temper is fried = trust crisis. Material conditions are the base, paralyzed action the result, identity clustering the compensation.
This is the social picture behind “individuals changing currency”: the old trust-currency system is failing as a whole; society has entered the credit-recasting period. In the recasting period, public opinion is the fastest currency, and human sincerity is the most expensive raw material — and the greatest danger is someone trying to counterfeit currency in the recasting.
IV. Five Pits in This Framework, and One Most Dangerous Spot The framework is useful, but five places demand braking, or the tool becomes a weapon.
First: don’t use Le Bon to pass verdicts on groups. “The crowd,” “the mob,” “human nature is evil” — Le Bon’s theory is good at describing the group’s destructive face, but it is forbidden to slap it onto groups as a label and then rationalize “groups don’t deserve trust.” The destructive face is real; the constructive face is also real. Using the theory to pass verdicts is reading the medical chart and refusing to look at the patient.
Second: don’t drop the material base. Tarde’s account of idea contagion is excellent, but don’t let it eclipse material conditions. Rich-poor, class, distribution are forever the base — they rarely detonate directly, but they hold up everything above. Analysis that talks only about ideas and never about matter floats away.
Third: don’t use Tocqueville as a prediction. The expectation gap explains “under what conditions unrest tends to arise”; it does not prophesy “eruption is certain.” He observed France at the end of the 18th century — an era without today’s media and institutions. The mechanism can be borrowed; the conclusions cannot be transported. Conditions in place do not equal event occurring — countless variables sit in between. Using it as a doomsday countdown is misuse.
Fourth: watch for the “general will” being hijacked. This is the most dangerous one. Rousseau said the social contract flows from the general will — but the general will is easily stolen by power. In a trust crisis, the people shouting “rebuild the social contract, restore public credibility” do not all want rebuilding — some want to use the crisis to seize power. Any narrative that channels “distrust” toward “we need a strongman to take charge” deserves one extra question: who benefits? And one further: all narratives that fly the flag of “rebuilding trust” while demanding the transfer of power get one question first — who supervises the “rebuilder”?
Fifth, the general rule: don’t read this as a doomsday prophecy. The credit-recasting period is the labor pain of one paradigm replacing another, not the end of civilization. Things are breaking: the old trust infrastructure is collapsing. Things are growing: verifiability, sincerity, eye-level communication, small trust circles — the new trust assets are appreciating (the five currents on the individual side are exactly these). The framework is an observation tool, not a disaster prophecy; whoever uses it to argue “society is finished” has used it wrong.
And one last line drawing the competence boundary: this framework applies only to group phenomena at the level of social trust. It does not apply to legal determinations or individual moral verdicts. It is an observation lens, not a judge.
V. The Group Recasts — What Does the Individual Do? Society covered, we must return to you. Readers of this site are not here to watch the spectacle; they are here for “what should I do” — however clearly the group half is explained, if it doesn’t land on the individual it is just another way of reading the news.
The recasting will not complete itself. Society does not become trustworthy on its own unless a new consensus base appears — and that base has a name: verifiability.
But a key clarification first, so the logic doesn’t collide: an individual doing trustworthy things does not automatically aggregate into social consensus — otherwise the “collective action problem” wouldn’t exist (that is exactly what Olson said in chapter two: individually rational actions do not automatically sum into collective outcomes).
Aggregation happens at a smaller scale: small trust circles. Inside a small circle, your trustworthy behavior is directly seen and directly rewarded — the free-rider problem doesn’t exist inside the circle; when you’re honest, circle members know at once and reciprocate at once. Between circles, connection and amplification happen through “verifiers”: a person verified by one circle is handed to another circle for further verification. So read the “rebar” metaphor this way: rebar doesn’t become a building by lying scattered on the ground — it first becomes rebar inside small structures, then gets welded together node by node by verifiers.
This is precisely the group projection of the individual side’s five currents: current four (small trust circles appreciate) handles “becoming rebar”; current five (occupying the verifier position) handles “welding.” Every new trust niche you occupy at the individual level — one transparent deal, one promise given without discount, one thing made public before it charges — is one piece of rebar in the recasting period.
One sentence to close:
Individuals are changing currency; the group awaits recasting. Every old banknote you exchange adds one load of material to society’s recasting; every new trust niche you raise is one piece of rebar for the recasting period — first becoming rebar in small circles, then welded together by verifiers.
VI. Era Observation Starts From This Essay This essay does not end on a conclusion. It ends at the beginning of a column.
What “Era Observation” will do is apply this framework over and over: no chasing hot-topic emotions; only analytical frameworks. Every collective event that leaves you “unable to read it” or “suffocating” can be placed into this signal → index → calibration → boundary structure, and taken apart for you — what it is, where it came from, where it goes, what you can do. It makes no prophecies. It gives you a ruler, and a lamp.
The column’s rhythm, with the rule stated plainly — target: one issue per month, with a floor: better late than padded. A column about trustworthiness owes its first act of trustworthiness to itself: never submit a half-finished draft. This sentence is written here for the people who trust this column most: rather late than padded.
One ruler has been placed in your hands. What to measure first is your call — what should the next issue take apart with this framework?
① Corporate trust collapses (what structure lies behind an Evergrande-style blowup) ② Public-opinion reversal events (how a Yan Dongping-style reversal gets pushed along)

I. Prologue: The Bewilderment of a Saturday Afternoon Saturday, 2 p.m. You turn off the alarm and roll over, satisfied. Curtains drawn shut, phone tilted above your face, thumb mechanically swiping through short videos — a cat getting startled into a jump, a clip of some middle-aged man teaching you to get rich overnight, an AI-generated “Einstein explains quantum mechanics” remix.
Three hours later, what you feel is not refreshment but a deeper fatigue. Not bodily tiredness — it’s the kind of emptiness seeping out from between your bones, worse than working overtime until 10 p.m. on a Thursday. You’re not even sure what you actually did. You “rested” for an entire weekend — so why are you not only tired, but tinged with a faint self-disgust?
Almost every modern person has asked themselves this question. And almost everyone finds the wrong answer.
The answer hides in two directions few people look at directly: you are resting in the wrong dimensions, and your resting environment is itself a higher-wattage drain machine.
II. Deep Dive: Dissecting “Pseudo-Rest” with the Inner Civilization Framework Energy determines cognition — the energy paradox of rest
We habitually equate “rest” with “not working.” That is cognitive residue left by the industrial age. Workers on an assembly line genuinely could recover by simply “shutting down” — their bodies were single-purpose energy-consumption machines, and stopping meant recharging.
The energy metabolism of knowledge workers doesn’t work that way. Your brain, while “resting” — scrolling feeds, bingeing shows, gaming — keeps running at considerable wattage. The dopamine system keeps responding to fresh pushes; the prefrontal cortex keeps judging “is this video worth another ten seconds”; every swipe is a micro cognitive decision. You think you’ve shut down the machine. In fact you’re idling — burning only 15–20% less energy than full-load work, with zero output.
This is the first truth about why modern rest makes people more tired: you never turned off the engine. You just shifted into neutral.
The environment loop — your “resting environment” is shaping you in reverse
The second truth is stealthier, and deadlier.
Your phone, your bedroom, your digital space — these so-called “resting environments” are, in essence, attention-hunting grounds meticulously engineered by algorithms. Every push notification, every red dot, every vibration activates your stress circuitry. You think you’re relaxing, but your nervous system has remained in a state of “light combat readiness.” Neuroscience has confirmed: merely having a device ringing with notifications nearby is enough to raise your cortisol levels — even if you never touch it.
This explains why you feel more tired after “lying flat with your phone” than after work: your body is lying flat, but your nervous system is still standing in the trench, rifle in hand, watching the enemy lines.
And once this “pseudo-rest” becomes the standard weekend procedure, the brain builds a despairing neural loop: rest = information overload + cognitive idling + dopamine emptiness. So the more you rest the tireder you get; the tireder you get, the less you want to do anything genuinely effective; and the less you want to do, the more you need cheap informational pleasure to fill the void — a negative feedback loop spiraling ever downward.
This is not a willpower failure. This is your environment working a shift job for the algorithm.
III. The Way Out: A Four-Dimensional Action Guide to “Real Rest” Since pseudo-rest is a multi-dimensional problem, breaking it requires multi-dimensional coordination. Below are field-tested strategies:
Energy dimension → restart charging at the mitochondrial level
Real rest concerns cellular-level energy metabolism, not sensory amusement. Concretely:
15 minutes of screen-free morning light: after waking, touch no screen; stand by a window or on a balcony and let natural light hit your retina. This switches off melatonin and resets the circadian rhythm — far more effective than one extra hour of sleep. The 4-7-8 breath (whenever fatigue hits): inhale 4 seconds, hold 7, exhale 8. Three rounds. This physiologically dampens sympathetic arousal — far more effective than five more minutes of short videos. The midday power break: not a nap — 5 minutes of high-density movement (push-ups, squats, jumping jacks). It boosts mitochondrial activity and extends your afternoon cognitive endurance by 40–60 minutes. Environment dimension → digital minimization
The “empty container” method: during rest hours, put the phone in another room, or into a timed locking box. Physical removal, not willpower. Design “theme rest days”: each weekend, pick one day as a “low-information day” — no short videos, no news, no social feeds. Replace them with a paper book, a long walk, a meal cooked with your own hands. Within a week or two you will feel a long-lost sense of the brain getting clean. Observation dimension → rebuild the mental model of “rest”
Replace “rest duration” with a “repair score”: after each activity, score how repaired you feel (0–10). You’ll be surprised to find two hours of short videos scores a 1, while one full long run scores an 8. That’s not a feeling — that’s data. Distinguish “passive recovery” from “active recovery”: passive recovery (scrolling, lying on the sofa) is merely shutdown; active recovery (walking, meditation, deep conversation with a person, making something by hand) is system optimization. Guarantee at least three sessions of active recovery per week. Tool dimension → use AI to help you rest
Counterintuitive but true: AI is the best rest coach.
Use prompts to have AI design your weekly energy management plan — not your time management plan. Have it track your “cognitive burnout index” and automatically remind you to switch states when you cross the threshold. Build an automated “attention audit” pipeline: once a month, have AI analyze your screen-time report, identifying which apps are “energy vampires” and which hours are your “high-energy windows.” This is not fleeing technology. This is turning technology from an exploiter into your health supervisor.
IV. The Sublimation: Redefining “Alertness” on the Algorithmic Hunting Ground Beneath the surface of “resting yet growing tired” hides a larger predicament of our era: rest itself has become alienated.
In an age where attention is worth more than oil, your “rest time” is not private territory — it is an open hunting ground. Capital and algorithms work hand in hand, with the shortest feedback loops, the highest dopamine doses, and the most precisely targeted content feeds, converting your “free time” into their “revenue.” Rest is no longer recovery; it has become another form of labor — working for the attention economy.
Realizing this is itself the first step of awakening.
Real rest is not lying flat, and not switching off work. It is seizing back control of your own physical and mental rhythms. You decide when to take input, when to produce output, when to zero out, when to upgrade. It is human subjectivity in the digital age: the shift from “being fed by algorithms” to “actively designing your own information metabolism.”
You don’t need to flee technology — you only need to put technology back in the place of a tool. You don’t need to be the algorithm’s enemy — you only need to shift your vantage from prey to hunter.
This is not a techniques course on “efficient rest.” It is an ultimate choice about “what makes a person human”: in a wilderness where even exhaustion gets packaged as a business model, can you still remain a clear-headed human being?
The old saying has never been more urgent — those who never rest will not succeed; and those who never learned how to rest are quietly losing this war of the era. True nobility was never about out-grinding everyone else. It is this: amid the smoke of information warfare filling the sky, still knowing at exactly which moment to pull the plug.

2 a.m. I’m staring at n8n’s workflow editor, two dozen drag-and-drop nodes snaking across the screen.
This tool, billed as a “low-code automation miracle,” consumed three evenings of my patience just to move a Markdown file from point A to point B. Dependency conflicts on install, a Docker image that wouldn’t pull, some node timing out for no reason. Every click of “test workflow” fed my cognitive bandwidth to an abstraction layer that should never have existed.
I stopped the n8n container. Then I wrote one line of Python.
shutil.copy(src, dst) Three lines of code. Zero dependencies. Zero configuration. Zero psychological overhead.
This is not a story about technology selection. It is a story about cognitive energy.
I. The “Efficiency Refugees” in Your Bookmarks How many “Must-learn AI tools for 2026” and “Ultimate guide to automation workflows” are lying in your browser bookmarks?
How much time do you spend each day scrolling productivity tutorials, comparing Notion vs Obsidian, agonizing over which Pomodoro app to use?
Our generation has fallen into an eerie paradox: we spend time studying efficiency tools in order to save time — and the time all gets spent on studying.
This is not a personal willpower problem. It is a systematic mismatch between your mental model and the algorithmic age.
When your “efficiency system” itself becomes the new cognitive burden, the tool has already consumed you. You are not “managing efficiency” — you are working for the productivity-tool companies, trading your attention for their DAU.
Real efficiency doesn’t need to be “managed.” It should be as natural as breathing: no dashboards, no sprint check-ins, no weekly reports.
II. The Toxicity of Tools: How Abstraction Layers Eat Your Cognitive Bandwidth Every abstraction layer charges you a “cognition tax.”
n8n taxes you: three evenings to learn its node API Airtable taxes you: its torturous formula syntax Zapier taxes you: monthly billing caps + step limits You think these tools “solve problems.” No — they manufacture an environment in which you can consume problems. Like the banquet in The Hunger Games: it looks like everything is on the table, while every dish quietly drains your digestion.
My switching philosophy is simple: if one line of code can solve it, never reach for a framework.
GitHub Actions replaced Jenkins. Git hooks replaced elaborate CI/CD panels. A bash script replaced n8n’s graphical workflow.
The price? Sacrificing a bit of “visual” vanity. What I got back: I know exactly what every line of code does. No magic. No abstraction. No 2 a.m. puzzling over “why did it do that?”
This is not “anti-tool.” This is the principle of cognitive transparency: if you cannot explain a tool’s core mechanism in three seconds, it is consuming your attention.
III. The Way Out: Code as a Cognitive Lever Many people say “I can’t program.” And as they say it, they are dragging n8n nodes with a mouse, or writing twenty layers of nested IFs in Excel formulas.
You are already programming. You’re just using the worst programming language ever invented — the mouse.
Switching from “visual tools” to “code” gives you three cognitive levers:
Lever one: remove the abstraction layer. When you type git push origin main, you know what you’re doing. When you click a “Sync” button, you’re guessing. Removing abstraction means going from “user” to “driver.”
{% blockquote %} The highest form of knowledge is being able to build it with your own hands. {% endblockquote %}
Lever two: versioned thinking. Code is versioned by nature. Every operation is recorded by Git; every rollback is a lesson. The operations inside GUI tools — the drags, the clicks, the selections — all vanish with the wind.
Lever three: the power of composition. A person who can write a shell script holds ten thousand keys. They can connect any two tools without depending on a third-party “integration marketplace.” The power of composition is not linear; it is exponential.
Concretely, for this blog’s home base:
Hugo static generation — the whole site compiles in 300 ms. No PHP backend, no database, no worry about getting hacked GitHub Actions auto-deploy — git push triggers the build, live in 60 seconds One Python script for article migration + Git push — replacing what once required n8n + Zapier + two webhooks The cost of this stack: zero. Runtime overhead: zero. Maintenance burden: zero.
IV. Tool Symbiosis: Humans Lead, Tools Assist I am not preaching that “all tools must die.” What I’m saying is: your mind should not be devoured by tools.
A good tool is like a scalpel — precise, transparent, entirely under your control. A bad tool is like a vending machine — you insert coins, press buttons, it dispenses things, and you will never know what happened in those three seconds inside.
The ultimate criterion for choosing a tool: does it let you think more clearly, or merely consume more comfortably?
When you write a script in Python, you are forced to understand the “why.” When you drag nodes in a GUI tool, you only learn “where to click.”
That is the dividing line between the “efficiency refugee” and the “efficiency citizen.”
Aphorisms
One rough line of Python is the exoskeleton of your cognition; ten thousand perfect saved articles are the tombstone of your attention.
Real efficiency is not doing more things. It is completing more of what truly matters, with less cognitive energy.
Your automation should not merely save time. It should be an investment of cognitive energy.
This very article was published through that “minimalist pipeline” of Hugo + Python + GitHub Actions. From writing the first word to pushing it live, I did not open a single “productivity tool.”
